Yes the Doppler effect is very vivid here (and yes I think 2 * step is correct). You can see the difference in length in the forward and backward readers. 

[quoted text / pattern omitted]

There is another pretty trivial way to adjust - use block moving slow salvo recipe. To clarify this, lets assume we have 15 gliders movement recipe from any point to any point. Now we always apply this recipe, and it takes exactly the same gliders which are always placed in (0, step size) range (as we don't use the +59 trick because we 0 mod 8 ). Now lets say we move the block not to (X, Y) but to (X, Y + 1). Because everything else remained constant, the *WSS recipe applied to (X, Y+1) will have latency of 8 ticks relative to (X, Y), 4 ticks because the SL moved 2 cells and the gliders fire with latency of 4, and another 4 ticks as the *WSS will be created 4 ticks bellow. 

Now if we agree with the above logic, I claim we can remove the 15 gliders constrain. The only thing that was really matter is that the last emitted glider from (X, Y) and (X, Y + 1) were 4 ticks apart (activated by the same reading head). Now if we have two block movements, one takes 10 and other 15, we just don't do anything for 5 glider emission timing. Doing nothing will equalize the timing as if we did something for 15 ticks instead of 10. 

I can say that my small tests with 59 step did show this is also working in practice, but yet again D59 is a bit different.

Yes, it isn't really a N-glider constraint, it's an "N-helix-cycle" constraint.  Generally speaking, adding a helix cycle will change the timing (by 40 or whatever, as shown in my last post) but it's easy to make adjustments on top of that.

Re: the "40" constant for 512-spaced recipes -- not surprisingly, moving the read-head spacing up to 514 also changes the timing differential for helix cycles from 40 to 42:

[quoted text / pattern omitted]
I think this means that for 118-step systems, the zero point I was worried about will never occur -- because the read heads can't be moved 40 steps closer together without colliding, and if they're moved farther apart, the distance between the upships increases in lockstep.  (And again, I agree that there was no reason to worry about the zero point anyway.)

Maybe there's some N-step system where the read heads can be moved close enough together to allow a zero point.  If so, it would be somewhat easier to work with, since recipes would all work the same no matter how many cycles they took.  But it would be a very special case, and it looks as if it won't be particularly difficult to factor in a per-cycle offset.

Hmm, I hadn't followed that line of thought far enough.  I suppose the range of caterloopillar periods is relatively limited anyway -- can't get below the base period defined by the repeat time and distance of the reading heads.  So every rational speed lower than c/4 is about as universal as it's possible to get, anyway.

In that case, an idea I had yesterday might be vaguely useful after all, at least as a sanity check.  Of the 8,313 monochromatic block-move recipes I posted way back when on the Serizawa thread, 820 of them are P2-even:

[quoted text / pattern omitted]
The same filter could also be applied to the larger monochromatic-all collection posted in the same message.  But I suppose NewGlue will be able to re-create all of these recipes in fairly short order.

[quoted text / pattern omitted]

Lets assume we want to get to speed m/n (where 4m < n) , this means our movement distance D = m * k and our period (the time between read1 and read2) P = n * k, where k is some positive large number. Now without any loss of generality, we can chose our k = 8l. so D = m * 8 * l and P = n * 8 * l. This means all our periods can be presumed dividable by 8, and all our movement distances as well. 

Let me prove we can get as close to c/4 as needed.

As we know our SL movement done by converting SL->Glider and Glider->SL. All the conversions/glider reflections take constant time (the same goes for the helix), and we can remain in glider state as long as it's necessary. Glider moves with c/4 so in total if we move N ticks with speed c/4 and some C (which is constant) ticks we don't move, our average speed (which is the caterloopillar speed) would be c/4 * (N / (N + C)), because we can make N as large as needed we can get any speed lower than c/4. 

Another nuance that is necessary to mention is that the distance between reading head and the next measuring from bottom of the first and top of the second can also remain constant (meaning our information in a way of SL and not glider remains SL for constant time). 

In other words, Our step is the distance that SL travels by one "read" lets call it D. The time it took to move the SL is ~4D because most of the time it was glider. The next reading head will come shortly after the first finished, so the time between the reads (i.e. the period itself) is ~4D. 

[quoted text / pattern omitted]

40 = 512 - 4 * 118. To get to zero point just use period 118 * 8. The zero point is very important place as we can't use any tricks regarding skips for movement purposes. c/8, c/16, c/24... etc are always zero points. Fortunately we don't need to use skips but only block movement recipes.

Got it -- thanks.  I knew something strange was going on there.  It was mostly Doppler-effect confusion on my part.

Here's a minor caveat, though.  At a zero point, there are a lot fewer adjustment options, but skipping helix cycles can still cause location changes.

Example:  you mentioned period 118*8 = 944.  This translates into a 590-cell spacing of the read heads -- period 944 = 2*590 - 2*118 due to the Doppler effect... the upship *WSS spacing is then 354 cells, since 944 = 2*354 + 2*118.

At this period, skipping one helix cycle produces an offset of -118 relative to no-skip, and skipping two cycles changes the location by -236 (or +118); you have to skip three cycles to see the zero point.  So even at c/8N periods, you still have to worry a little bit about which cycle the trigger glider comes from.

import golly as g 

def MakeBackwardSalvo(distance):
	
	backHelixSL = g.parse("bo$obo$obo$bo!", 191, 1137)
	backHelixSL2GliderWSS = g.parse("bobo$o$o3bo$o$o2bo$3o!", 186, 1130)
	backHelixReflect = g.parse("bobo$o$o$o2bo$3o10$7bobo$10bo$6bo3bo$10bo$7bo2bo$8b3o!", 127, 955)
	backHelixGlider2SL = g.parse("b2o$3o$3o$2obo$b3o$2bo!", 191, 781)

	backErasingReflectorWSS = g.parse("bobo$o$o3bo$o3bo$o$o2bo$3o62$16bobo$15bo$15bo3bo$15bo3bo$15bo$15bo2bo$15b3o!", 87, 833)
	backSL = g.parse("b2o$o2bo$obo$bo!", 25, 734)
	backFrontPart = g.parse("74b2o$73b3o$73b2obo$74b3o$75bo76$31bobo$30bo$30bo3bo$30bo3bo$30bo$30bo2bo$30b3o55$41b2o$41b3o$41b3o$40bob2o$40b3o$41bo7$20bobo$19bo$19bo3bo$19bo$19bo2bo$19b3o31$bobo$o$o$o2bo$3o50$10bobo$9bo$9bo3bo$9bo$9bo2bo$9b3o70$39bobo$38bo$38bo3bo$38bo3bo$38bo$38bo2bo$38b3o81$73bobo$72bo$72bo3bo$72bo3bo$72bo$72bo2bo$72b3o!", 0, 360)
	backReflectingPart = g.parse("27bobo$26bo$26bo$26bo2bo$26b3o24$17bobo$16bo$16bo3bo$16bo3bo$16bo$16bo2bo$16b3o23$15bobo$18bo$14bo3bo$14bo3bo$18bo$15bo2bo$16b3o5$b2o$3o$3o$3o$2obo$b3o$2bo!", 88, 210)
	backBackPart = g.parse("6bobo$9bo$9bo$9bo$6bo2bo$7b3o15$bobo$4bo$o3bo$o3bo$4bo$bo2bo$2b3o!", 30, 0)
	
	d = (distance - 118) / 2
	g.putcells(backHelixSL, d, d * 3)
	g.putcells(backHelixSL2GliderWSS, d, d * 3)
	g.putcells(backHelixReflect)
	g.putcells(backHelixGlider2SL, d, -d * 3)
	g.putcells(backErasingReflectorWSS)
	g.putcells(backSL, -d, -d)
	g.putcells(backFrontPart, -d, -d)
	g.putcells(backReflectingPart, 0, -4 * d)
	g.putcells(backBackPart, -d, -d * 7)

def MakeForwardSalvo(distance):
	frontHelixSL = g.parse("6bo$5bobo$5bobo$6bo2$b2o7b2o$o2bo5bo2bo$b2o7b2o2$6bo$5bobo$5bobo$6bo!", 0, 0)
	frontHelixSL2GliderWSS = g.parse("3o$o2bo$o$o3bo$o$bobo!", 9, 15)
	frontHelixReflect = g.parse("2b3o$bo2bo$4bo$o3bo$4bo$bobo8$9b3o$8bo2bo$11bo$7bo3bo$7bo3bo$11bo$8bobo!", 61, 60)
	frontHelixGlider2SL = g.parse("2bo$b3o$2obo$3o$3o$b2o!", 4, 126)

	frontErasingReflectorWSS = g.parse("2bo$b3o$2obo$3o$3o$3o$b2o59$14bo$13b3o$12b2obo$12b3o$12b3o$12b3o$13b2o!", 91, 93)
	frontSL = g.parse("bo$obo$o2bo$b2o!", 145, 194)
	frontFrontPart = g.parse("25bo$24b3o$23b2obo$23b3o$23b3o$24b2o68$37bo$36b3o$36bob2o$37b3o$37b3o$37b3o$37b2o8$3o$o2bo$o$o3bo$o$bobo39$24bo$23b3o$23bob2o$24b3o$4b3o17b3o$3bo2bo17b3o$6bo17b2o$2bo3bo$2bo3bo$6bo$3bobo!", 139, 264)
	frontReflectingPart = g.parse("7bo$6b3o$5b2obo$5b3o$5b3o$5b3o12bo$6b2o11b3o$18b2obo$18b3o$19b2o14$2bo$b3o$2obo$3o$3o$b2o!", 82, 460)
	frontBackPart = g.parse("11b3o$11bo2bo$11bo$11bo3bo$11bo$12bobo4$3o$o2bo$o$o3bo$o3bo$o$bobo!", 145, 542)
	frontErasingReflector = g.parse("bo$3o$ob2o$b3o$b2o!", 122, 488)

	d = (distance - 118) / 2
	d_3 = int(d / 3)

	g.putcells(frontHelixSL, -d, -d)
	g.putcells(frontHelixSL2GliderWSS, -d, -d)
	g.putcells(frontHelixReflect)
	g.putcells(frontHelixGlider2SL, -d, d)
	g.putcells(frontErasingReflectorWSS)

	g.putcells(frontSL, d, d)
	g.putcells(frontFrontPart, d, d)
	g.putcells(frontReflectingPart, 0, 2 * d)
	g.putcells(frontBackPart, d, 3 * d)
	g.putcells(frontErasingReflector, d - d_3, d + 3 * d_3)
	
operation = g.getstring("Enter even step size: \n F100 - 100 forarward \n B100 - 100 backward", "F100")

salvoType = ""

if operation[0] == 'B' or operation[0] == 'b':
	salvoType = "backward"
	try:
		step = int(operation.replace("B", "").replace("b", ""))
	except:
		g.exit("step must be integer")
	
if operation[0] == 'F' or operation[0] == 'f':
	salvoType = "forward"
	try:
		step = int(operation.replace("F", "").replace("f", ""))
	except:
		g.exit("step must be integer")

if salvoType == "":
	g.exit("Couldn't recogine command")
	
if step % 2 != 0:
	g.exit("Step must be even number")

if salvoType == "forward":
	g.new(operation)
	MakeForwardSalvo(step)
else:
	g.new(operation)
	MakeBackwardSalvo(step)

g.fit()

Looks good!  I did a little testing and didn't find anything wrong, except maybe that the script will cheerfully build impossibly short-step spines.  Thanks to the new rather slow *WSS+G -> block+G, it doesn't look like any steps shorter than B96 will work.  Forward spines could be tightened up a good bit more -- F72 works, but F70 doesn't.

In the script, the default step is 100.  Are there subtle limitations that mean that the minimum step should really be 98 or 100, not 96?

[quoted text / pattern omitted]

I chose default to clarify the usage (the first time the user run the script as is, and see it working - this makes his life so much easier). I just made sure 100 is working, and it was chosen because it's round number. I was mainly concentrating for large numbers to work. 

I'm surprised the minimal back step is so high. I really have issues with the back design, it's somewhat awkward, but nevertheless working. I think some tweaking should make it possible to reduce both spines to ~15 in optimal case after a lot of effort. 

I don't have any theory on how to optimize the self destruct, I used pure greedy algorithm (each block will erase maximum it can). For the back spine, the self destruct is 1 to 1 (each *WSS has another *WSS to delete it). 

It would be nice to modify the script to make *WSS salvo by input period. Anyway for now I'm switching to write slow salvo LifeAPI *WSS search.

Luckily eaters are a lot more useful for Herschel conduits than for engineless Caterpillars.  They aren't high on the list of components for 3SL *WSS seeds -- though quite possibly including them would add enough new search space that a 2SL *WSS seed might show up.

Anyway, there's an integral with the missing orientation.  In Spartan circuitry it's very often possible to substitute an integral for a standard eater, if it's eating a glider... or substitute a hat if the tail end is being used as a rock -- that orientation of hat also happens to be available.

However, if P2-even slow salvos were going to be used to construct Spartan circuitry, it would be necessary to search a few levels deeper anyway. I've added Glue++ (glue on c++ using LifeAPI), to the Glue repository.

It uses OpenMP for parallel threading (comes with gcc and most modern compilers - but you need to add flag -fopenmp). 

There is some memory issue that causes the application to take too much memory for some reason. I seem to clean everything correctly and the recipes are kept in a tree with optimized format for memory. So depth 11 was the limit at my machine. 

The results are reported in the same library as the exe, and got a lot of false positives. But the report shouldn't miss *WSS if it appeared, so cleaning the results with python script is necessary. 

The last layer reported 14K results (with a lot of junk). 

It looks like the memory leak fix is crucial to get enough results.

I've improved the Glue++ by order of magnitude in speed and memory. 

Here are some tricks I used: 

In target search one should prefer shuffled data, instead of one next to other cell. The shuffled data cleaned much quicker statistically speaking (there are much more neighboring ON cells than two ON cells with some (dx, dy)).

The TargetLocator could be cheated by some random "*WSS like" pattern that appeared quickly and disappeared again. Making extra check  after 4 generation makes the chances much lower for false positives. 

Having tree of glider locations can be unpredictable, so storing the tree inside flat vector makes it much more controllable. 

This one is dvgrn inspired trick: I clean the hash table of existing pattern when it gets too large. This will cause some of the patterns to repeat, but saves memory and time (from some point the request for the hash table becomes the most intensive operation). I've picked the value to be large enough so the quality will not deteriorate quickly. 

Another trick is to limit the population. This is both quality and performance improvement. The more messy the pattern is the less chances edgy *WSS will come out of it, and the less chances it will repeat again so hashing it is useless. So limiting the population will allow to save on memory and improves quality. 

Now after those introductions, what previously took about 5 hours and took 2G is now taking half hour and takes 100M, reporting better quality results. 

NOTE Memory is still major limitation, as I didn't implemented other dvgrn's trick to search with higher depths, inside some high quality results of lower depth. 
--- 

Switching to python parser now.

EDIT I've introduced few key features:

1. Save and load the data of each search depth. Now other slow salvo searches are possible using the same search tree just by loading the tree. 

2. Every 500 results are reported, so even if something went wrong, the last run results will be available. 

3. The most important is the option to search for edge shooters but without updating the search tree, thus getting one search depth deeper without paying any price for it. Similar to dvgrn's proposal to search inside limited depth, only with depth = 1. 

As the memory playing less of an issue, the run time starts to play. Hopefully finding all the edge shooters in the scope of the run.
